newsitem.title: INDIA: Punjab brushes off separatism as "bad nightmare".
newsitem.headline: Punjab brushes off separatism as "bad nightmare".

text.p: India's northern Punjab state election campaign ended on Thursday amid solid grass-roots support for a pro-Sikh party ahead of Friday's key polls.

The election to the 117-seat state assembly will be the first polls in Punjab in nearly two decades not overshadowed by Sikh separatists fighting for a separate homeland called Khalistan, or Land of the Pure.
Prakash Singh Badal's resurgent Akali Dal party is widely expected to win the polls and defeat the Congress party, which has ruled for five years.
Badal is Punjab's former chief minister.
The Akali Dal has been accused by Congress of fanning Sikh separatism.
Peace has largely returned to the region after the decade-long separatist revolt, in which more than 20,000 people died.
State polls in 1992, which revived local democracy, were held amid fear and heavy security.
India has poured in paramilitary troops to oversee the elections, sealing off Punjab's borders with Pakistan and neighbouring states.
But there were no signs of security forces for miles along the road to Tarn Taran, once a bedrock of insurgency.
"This road was (once) controlled by the security forces," said a village member. "Those villages over there were run by the boys."
For most village elders in Sheron, the dozens of separatist guerrilla chiefs who once flourished in the village were "boys who fought Delhi's oppression".
Their fondness for Badal, a turbanned Sikh leader who has been in and out of jail while fighting Indian governments, was evident.
The quiet support for Badal is shored up by his surprising alliance with the rightwing Hindu nationalist Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP), a critic of separatism.
Badal directs his ammunition at the Congress party, which ruled India for most of the decade-long Sikh rebellion.
"The Congress tried to divide Hindus and Sikhs," said Pargat Singh, a 65-year-old farmer. "Badal is uniting them."
Nationwide, Sikhs form two percent of India's 936 million people against some 82 percent for Hindus. In Punjab the two communities are more or less equal in number, more so in the cities.
